ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: The report to the 20th National Congress proposed the “seed industry revitalization action.” Rapeseed is an important oil crop. Screening breeding materials with excellent traits and exploring the corresponding genetic mechanisms are of great significance for creating new high-yield and high-quality varieties. Chinese scientists treated wild-type rapeseed (green leaves) with a mutagen and obtained a new-leaf etiolation mutant (yellowed leaves). The mutant was crossed with the wild type, and the results are shown in Figure Jia, from which it can be inferred that the recessive trait is yellowed leaves. Rapeseed male-sterile line A was used as the female parent and crossed with fertile line R to obtain hybrid rapeseed seeds S (heterozygotes), making large-scale cultivation of hybrid rapeseed possible. Line A1 has normal fertility, and its other traits are the same as A. A and A1 are crossed, and the first filial generation is still line A; thus A can be propagated in large quantities. In the process of propagating A in large quantities, A can become impure due to contamination by pollen from other lines, thereby affecting the purity of seed S and causing rapeseed yield reduction. The new-leaf etiolation phenotype of rapeseed is easy to identify and has no significant effect on yield. Scientists envisioned using the new-leaf etiolation trait to improve the purity of seed S. In the breeding process, first through a series of operations, A1 with new-leaf etiolation was obtained. The breeding procedure for using yellowed A1 to produce seed S is shown in Figure Bing. In Figure Bing, the green-leaf male-sterile progeny of plant A is crossed with yellowed A1. About what proportion of the total first filial generation are the screened-out yellowed A plants?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: Figure Jia shows that the P generation is wild-type green leaves crossed with yellowed leaves, and all F1 show wild type; after F1 selfing, in F2 there are 980 wild-type plants and 346 yellowed-leaf plants, with a ratio of about 3:1. Figure Bing shows that in the breeding procedure, plant A first receives pollen from yellowed A1, producing green-leaf male-sterile plants; then yellowed A plants are screened out, and related steps with yellowed A1 are continued for propagation; finally yellowed A plants receive pollen from R to harvest seed S. Reasoning: From Figure Jia, with all F1 wild type and F2 about 3:1, it can be judged that yellowed leaves are a recessive trait. Let the green-leaf allele be G and the yellowed allele be g; then the genotype of yellowed A1 is gg. In Figure Bing, after plant A receives pollen from yellowed A1, the obtained green-leaf male-sterile progeny, because the paternal yellowed A1 can only provide g gametes, and the progeny show green leaves, should have genotype Gg. This green-leaf male-sterile progeny is then crossed with yellowed A1, namely Gg × gg, and among the offspring, 1/2 are Gg green leaves and 1/2 are gg yellowed. Also because the stem states that the first filial generation from crossing A and A1 is still line A, the yellowed progeny among them are yellowed A plants. Therefore, the screened-out yellowed A plants account for about 1/2 of the total first filial generation.
